detaileddescription.para: The PDI specification tree is expressed in YAML. This reference documents each key of the tree in its own section, named by the full path that leads to it from the root of the tree.

The paths follow these conventions:
a dot . separates a key from the key that contains it, e.g. logging.output.file is the file key of the output mapping of the logging mapping at the root of the tree,
a name between angle brackets is a key whose name you choose, e.g. data.<data_name> is any key of the data mapping,
[*] stands for any element of a sequence, e.g. include[*],
where a key accepts either a single value or a sequence of such values, the paths below it are written for the single value, and they apply to each element of the sequence alike.

Datatypes and $-expressions can be found at many places in the tree, including in the configuration of plugins. Each is documented once, in <datatype> and $-expressions, and the paths of their keys start from the datatype itself, e.g. <array>.size is the size key of a datatype whose type is array, wherever that datatype appears.
The root of the specification tree is a mapping. Keys not listed in this reference are ignored at the root of the tree.

sect1.para: Optional. Other YAML files, or subtrees of files, that hold parts of the same specification tree.

The value is either a single include directive or a sequence of include directives. An include directive is either:
a scalar, the path of a file whose root is included, a shortcut for a mapping whose file is that scalar and whose subtree is empty,
a mapping with both an include.file and an include.subtree key, and no other key.

An included tree has the same format as the root of the specification tree. Its include, types, metadata, data, plugin_path and plugins keys are taken into account, while its logging key is ignored. The keys under these sections must not be repeated: a type, a data, a metadata or a plugin defined in two files is an error.
The same file can be included twice (diamond include) but recursive inclusion is an error.

sect2.title: Example of include
sect2.para: is interpreted as if it was:

sect1.para: Required in a mapping include directive. A scalar, the path of the file to include. The path is interpreted relative to the working directory of the execution.
Required in a mapping include directive. A scalar, the ypath of the subtree to include from include.file, empty for the root of the file.

The subtree ypath is expanded according to the ypath specification of paraconf:
access to a mapping element using the dot syntax: e.g. .map.key
access to a sequence element using square brackets (indices are 0-based): e.g. .seq[1]
access to a mapping element key using braces (indices are 0-based): e.g. .map{1}
access to a mapping element value by index using chevrons: e.g. .map<1>

Optional. The configuration of the logger of PDI. It is only read from the root file, not from included ones. Each plugin has its own logger, configured by the logging key of its own configuration, with the same keys as below (see plugins.<plugin_name>.logging).

The value is either:
a scalar, a shortcut for a mapping whose only key is logging.level with that value,
a mapping with the keys below.

Optional. A scalar, the verbosity level of the logger. It can be set to (from the most to the least verbose):
"trace" - shows a log for every step of the execution, to debug the library itself,
"debug" - shows a log when a normal situation of the execution might be useful to understand the behavior of the library,
"info" - shows a log when a normal situation of the execution is likely useful to understand the behavior of the library,
"warn" - shows a log when a very likely invalid situation has been detected by the library (user input that is technically valid, but very unusual for example),
"error" - shows a log when an invalid situation has been detected by the library (invalid user input, invalid hardware behaviour, etc.),
"off" - logs are disabled.
By default, the level is info for PDI and the level of PDI for a plugin.
Optional. A scalar, the spdlog pattern of a log line.

The pattern is parsed by the spdlog library (see https://github.com/gabime/spdlog/wiki/3.-Custom-formatting). It specifies the format of the whole line, so it should contain v, the logged message itself.

PDI introduces a new special flag, %{<REF>}, where <REF> is the REFERENCE part of a $-expressions without its leading $ (with an optional format specification). It is evaluated just after all plugins have been initialized.

By default, the pattern is (where n is PDI or a plugin name): [%T][%n]***%^%l%$:%v for serial execution and: [%T][MPI%{MPI_COMM_WORLD_rank:06d}][%n]***%^%l%$:%v when the MPI plugin is loaded. The pattern of a plugin defaults to that of PDI.
Optional. A mapping, the destinations of the logs, with the keys below.
Optional. A scalar, the path of a file where to write the logs.
Optional. A scalar, on or off, whether to write the logs on the standard output. Only the exact value off disables the console, any other value enables it.
By default, it is off when logging.output.file is defined and on otherwise.
Optional. A mapping, the user-defined datatypes.
A <datatype>, the definition of the datatype named <type_name>. <type_name> can then be used as the value of <datatype>.type anywhere a datatype is expected.
A user-defined datatype cannot reuse the name of an existing datatype.
Optional. A mapping, the metadata exposed by the application. PDI keeps a copy of the value of a metadata when it is shared, so that it can be referenced in $-expressions afterwards.
A <datatype>, the type of the metadata named <data_name>.
A name can only be defined once among all metadata and data keys.
Optional. A mapping, the data exposed by the application. Unlike for metadata, PDI only keeps a reference to a data while it is shared.
A <datatype>, the type of the data named <data_name>.
A name can only be defined once among all metadata and data keys.
Optional. A scalar or a sequence of scalars, the path to directories where PDI should search for plugins.

PDI takes the first match, searching the directories of the PDI_PLUGIN_PATH environment variable first, then those of plugin_path, then the directory where PDI installs its plugins, and finally the system library path.
Optional. A mapping, the plugins to load.

The configuration of the plugin named <plugin_name>, which PDI loads. Its content depends on the plugin: have a look at the plugins documentation to see the specification tree each accepts. It can be empty (~) for a plugin that needs no configuration.
A plugin can only be loaded once, even across included files.
Optional. The configuration of the logger of the plugin, with the same format as logging. This key is handled by PDI for every plugin whose configuration is a mapping.

A datatype represents the memory layout and interpretation of data exposed by the application in the data store. It is the value of types.<type_name>, metadata.<data_name> and data.<data_name>, and of many keys of the plugins.

A datatype is either:
a scalar, the name of a type, a shortcut for a mapping with a single <datatype>.type key whose value is that scalar,
a mapping, whose <datatype>.type key identifies the type, and whose other keys depend on that type.
The paths of the keys that only some types accept start with the name of the type between angle brackets: <array>.size is the size key of a datatype whose type is array.

sect2.title: Example of <datatype>
sect2.para: is interpreted as if it was:

sect1.para: Required. A scalar, the name of the type.
It can be the name of a user-defined datatype (see types.<type_name>), of a type that a plugin makes available, or one of the following.

entry.para: a memory address where data is actually stored
a structure whose members are placed explicitly
a C struct or C++ class using the default C memory layout
the C unsigned long long type
the C int8_t, int16_t, int32_t, int64_t types
the C uint8_t, uint16_t, uint32_t, uint64_t types
the C intmax_t and uintmax_t types
the C intptr_t and uintptr_t types

sect1.para: The C types of the <stdint.h> and <stddef.h> headers can also be written with their _t suffix (int32_t, int_fast8_t, ptrdiff_t...), except for size_t that only exists in that form.
The Fortran types are only available when PDI is built with Fortran support.
Optional. Anything (scalar, sequence or mapping), the value of the attribute <attribute_name> of the datatype.
Attributes can be added to any datatype given as a mapping. They are not interpreted by PDI, but plugins can read them.

Optional. An integer-valued $-expressions, the Fortran kind parameter of a Fortran character, integer, logical or real type, e.g. integer(kind=...). If missing or 0, the default kind of the Fortran implementation is used.
A <datatype> whose <datatype>.type is array, a potentially multi-dimensional array.

Required. An integer-valued $-expressions or a sequence of them, the size of the array in each dimension (C order). A single expression is a shortcut for a sequence with a single element, a one-dimensional array.
Required. A <datatype>, the type of the elements of the array.

Optional, deprecated. An integer-valued $-expressions or a sequence of them, the number of elements to actually use in each dimension (slicing). If specified, it must have the same number of elements as <array>.size. It defaults to the full array size in each dimension.

Optional, deprecated. An integer-valued $-expressions or a sequence of them, the index of the first element to actually use in each dimension (slicing). If specified, it must have the same number of elements as <array>.size, and <array>.subsize must be specified too. It defaults to the first (0) element in each dimension.
Optional, deprecated. "C" or "c", the order of the dimensions. Only C order is supported and specifying it is deprecated.
A <datatype> whose <datatype>.type is pointer, a memory address where data is actually stored.
Required. A <datatype>, the type of the referenced elements.
A <datatype> whose <datatype>.type is record, a structure whose members are placed explicitly.
Required. An integer-valued $-expressions, the overall size of the record in bytes, including potential padding.
Optional. A mapping, the members of the record.
A <datatype> given as a mapping with an additional <record>.members.<member_name>.disp key, the member named <member_name> and its type.
Required. An integer-valued $-expressions, the offset in bytes of the member from the base address of the record.
A <datatype> whose <datatype>.type is struct, a C struct or C++ class using the default C memory layout.
Optional. An ordered mapping, i.e. a sequence of mappings with a single key each, the members of the struct in order.
A <datatype>, the type of the member named <member_name>.
A <datatype> whose <datatype>.type is tuple, a sequence of unnamed elements.

Optional. An integer-valued $-expressions, the overall size of the tuple in bytes, including potential padding. It must be specified if and only if the elements have a <tuple>.elements[*].disp. If omitted, the minimum size that fits all elements is used.
Required. A sequence, the elements of the tuple in order.
A <datatype>, the type of an element of the tuple, with an optional additional <tuple>.elements[*].disp key when it is given as a mapping.

Optional. An integer-valued $-expressions, the offset in bytes of the element from the base address of the tuple. Either all elements or none of them must have a disp key. If they have none, each element is placed at the minimum offset that does not lead to overlaps.

sect1.title: $-expressions
sect1.para: A $-expression is a scalar whose content matches the following grammar:
The rules for evaluating an expression are close to those of BASH for example.
In addition to raw text, a STRING_LITERAL can contain references to the string value of some data in the store as well as the result of an operation by enclosing it inside a dollar-parenthesis $().

An OPERATION can include logical and arithmetic operators grouped by parenthesis. The basic terms manipulated in an operation can be integer literals, floating-point literals or references to the value of some data in the store. An integer literal is decimal, hexadecimal if it starts with 0x or octal if it starts with 0 (010 is 8). A literal that contains a dot . is a floating-point literal.

A REFERENCE is introduced by a dollar $ sign and optionally enclosed in curly braces {, }. Its value is that of the data or metadata with the associated name. It is always a good idea to have referenced values in the metadata section as it prevents dangling references. Value formatting can be applied using a FMT format_spec string by adding a colon : followed by the format_spec just before the closing bracket } (see: https://fmt.dev/latest/syntax.html#grammar-token-format_spec). A direct reference is possible as well as sub-references to:
array elements using the square brackets [, ] operator,
record member using dot . operator.

Where a value is expected (and not only an integer or a string), a YAML sequence or mapping whose elements are $-expressions is accepted too:
a sequence is array-valued if all its elements have the same type and tuple-valued otherwise,
a mapping is record-valued, each key naming a member.
In addition, an integer can be interpreted as a string or as a boolean value where zero is interpreted as false and any other value as true.

The following strings can also be interpreted as a boolean integer values:
true (1): y, Y, yes, Yes, YES, true, True, TRUE, on, On, ON.
false (0): n, N, no, No, NO, false, False, FALSE, Off, OFF.
